seo.title: Antony (Anthony) the Great: the desert, the demons, his sayings
seo.description: Who Antony the Great was, in plain words: the desert, the demons, his miracles and sayings, and his feast days East and West, with sources.

who: Antony was the son of a wealthy Christian family in Egypt. At eighteen or twenty he gave away his land and went to live alone, first near his village and then deep in the desert. So many followed him that he is called the father of monks. He died in 356, about 105 years old.

To the people of his village
Nearly twenty, in an old fort
Bread let down twice a year

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 251. At Coma in Egypt, today **Qiman al-Arus, near Beni Suef**.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At home, with wealthy Christian parents. He would not learn letters, and did not care to mix with other boys. He went to church with his parents and kept what he heard read.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **356**, on his inner mountain near the Red Sea, aged about 105. The Monastery of St Antony stands there today. The Coptic Synaxarium says 355.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: In secret, by his two companions, as he had told them. Athanasius says no one else knew the place.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Antony the Great** in the East. **Saint Anthony, Abbot** in the Catholic calendar. **Antony of Egypt** in Anglican and Lutheran calendars. The Coptic Church calls him “the father of all monks”.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and the Coptic Church. The Church of England, the Episcopal Church and the ELCA keep his day too.

facts.label: Patron of
facts.text: Christian monasticism, and also butchers, gravediggers, basket makers, brush makers and animals, says Britannica. In Greece, the town of **Veria**.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: An old monk, often with a pig and a small bell. He holds a T-shaped staff, as in the painting at the top. The T, the Greek letter tau, is called St Anthony's cross. Painters from Bosch to Dalí painted **his temptation by demons**.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Seven letters in Coptic to monasteries, says Jerome. They survive in Latin. In 1907 the Catholic Encyclopedia thought it “premature to decide” if they are his.

portrait.alt: An icon on gold: Saint Antony with a long white beard, in a dark blue monk's hood marked with a cross and a brown cloak, holds a staff and an open scroll with Greek writing
portrait.credit: Saint Antony, Cretan icon, said to be 16th century. Dionysiou Monastery, Mount Athos. Public domain.
portrait.caption: An icon from Crete, said to be of the 16th century, at the Dionysiou Monastery on Mount Athos. He wears a monk's hood marked with a cross and holds a staff and an open scroll. Public domain.

typeNote: Light-hearted here means the settled joy Athanasius saw in his face. In Cassian's Conferences he is also named for The Watcher, one of the test's seven roles, among those “joined most closely to God by the silence of solitude”.

west.text: **Catholic** memorial, as Saint Anthony, Abbot. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **ELCA**, who keep Pachomius the same day. Not in the **Missouri Synod**'s calendar.

east.text: **Russian Church**, which keeps 17 January on the old calendar. Also the **Coptic Church**, whose 22 Toba falls here in most years.

feasts.note: East and West keep the same day. Churches on the old calendar count it 13 days later, so their 17 January falls on 30 January. Athanasius does not say what day he died.

traits.title: cheerful
traits.text: Strangers could pick him out of a crowd of monks. He was no taller or broader than the rest. They knew him by the calm in his face. “He was never disturbed, for his soul was at peace; he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous.”

traits.title: even after twenty years alone
traits.text: When friends broke down the door of his fort, he came out neither fat nor thin. His soul was just as steady. “It was neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection.”

traits.title: ready to learn
traits.text: He bowed his head to bishops and priests. When a deacon came to him, he gave way to the deacon in prayer. He often asked questions and listened, and “if any one said anything that was useful he confessed that he was profited.”

traits.title: quick-witted
traits.text: Philosophers came to mock him because he had never learned letters. He asked them which comes first, mind or letters. They said mind. “Whoever, therefore, hath a sound mind hath not need of letters.”

traits.title: gentle with the troubled
traits.text: A young man of rank, possessed by a demon, was brought to him. Antony prayed with him all night. At dawn the young man shoved him, and those who brought him were angry. Antony said, “Be not angry with the young man, for it is not he, but the demon which is in him.” The young man was healed.

said.lede: Almost everything we know comes from one book. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, wrote the Life of Antony within a few years of his death. He says he had seen Antony many times.

quotes.q: And it was as if a physician had been given by God to Egypt. For who in grief met Antony and did not return rejoicing?
He was exceedingly meek and philanthropic, prudent and manly; cheerful in conversation and friendly in disputations, even when others used the controverted topics as occasion for strife.
quotes.who: Sozomen, a church historian born about 400

quotes.q: …speaking of Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name was in high repute among Thy servants, though up to that time not familiar to us.
quotes.who: Augustine, in Milan about 386, on first hearing of him

quotes.q: We see nothing but tenderness and love of men in his character…
quotes.who: Archibald Robertson, who edited the Life in 1892 and found some of its stories silly

cite.text: Introduction to the Life of Antony

moments.title: One verse
moments.text: His parents died when he was eighteen or twenty, leaving him their land and a little sister. Less than six months later, in church, he heard Christ tell the rich man to sell what he had and give to the poor. “Antony, as though God had put him in mind of the Saints, and the passage had been read on his account, went out immediately from the church”. He gave his land to the villagers and sold the rest for the poor. He kept a little for his sister, until he heard “be not anxious for the morrow”. Then he gave that away too, and placed her with a community of virgins.

moments.title: Like a bee
moments.text: No monk yet knew the far desert, so he lived near his village. He copied an old hermit in the next village. Whenever he heard of a good man, he went to find him, “like the prudent bee”. He noted what each did best: one man's kindness, another's prayer, another's freedom from anger. Then he tried to have them all.

moments.title: Beaten in the tombs
moments.text: He shut himself in a tomb, and a friend brought him bread. One night demons beat him until he lay as if dead. His friend carried him to the village church, but at midnight Antony asked to be carried back. Alone again, he saw the roof open and a ray of light come down, and the pain left him. He asked, “Where wert Thou? Why didst Thou not appear at the beginning to make my pains to cease?” A voice answered, “Antony, I was here, but I waited to see thy fight; wherefore since thou hast endured, and hast not been worsted, I will ever be a succour to thee, and will make thy name known everywhere.”

moments.title: Twenty years in a fort
moments.text: He ran past gold lying in the road, crossed the river, and walled himself into an old fort full of creeping things. Bread was let down to him twice a year. Visitors outside heard din and voices within. After nearly twenty years his friends broke the door down. Cells soon rose even in the mountains, and “the desert was colonised by monks”.

moments.title: In his best clothes
moments.text: When the persecution under Maximinus came, he went to Alexandria to stand by the martyrs. He longed to die for Christ, but he would not hand himself in. He served the confessors in the mines and prisons. The judge ordered every monk out of the court and the city. The others hid. Antony “washed his garment, and stood all next day on a raised place before them, and appeared in his best before the governor.”

moments.title: Further into the desert
moments.text: When crowds would not leave him alone, a voice sent him into the inner desert. He travelled three days and nights with a band of Saracens to a high mountain with a cold spring and a few palm trees. “Recognising it as his own home, he remained in that place for the future.” He grew his own grain, so the brothers need not carry bread to him.

moments.title: Against the Arians
moments.text: The Arians claimed he agreed with them, and he was angry. Called by the bishops, he came down to Alexandria and taught the crowds that the Son of God is not a created being. Pagans and their priests came to the church asking to see “the man of God”. As many became Christians in those few days, says Athanasius, as in a year. When some tried to keep the crowds off him, he said calmly that there were no more of them than of the demons he wrestled on his mountain.

moments.title: Letters from emperors
moments.text: Constantine and his sons wrote to him as to a father. At first he did not want the letters read. “Do not be astonished if an emperor writes to us, for he is a man; but rather wonder that God wrote the Law for men and has spoken to us through His own Son.” In the end he wrote back. He told them to remember the judgment to come, and to care for justice and the poor.

miracles.lede: The Life is full of healings and wonders. Athanasius says Antony “healed not by commanding, but by prayer and speaking the name of Christ”. He wrote with care, he says, so that no one would disbelieve:

pledge.q: …in all points being mindful of the truth, that no one should disbelieve through hearing too much, nor on the other hand by hearing too little should despise the man.

items.title: Fronto
items.text: Fronto, an officer of the court, bit his own tongue, and his eyes were in danger. He came to the mountain and asked Antony to pray. Antony told him to go, and he would be healed. But Fronto stayed on for days. So Antony told him he would see the sign in Egypt. He believed and went.
items.quote: as soon as he set eyes on Egypt his sufferings ceased

items.title: The girl from Busiris
items.text: A girl from Busiris in Tripolitania had a hideous illness, and she was paralysed. Her parents brought her with a party of monks, and waited outside the mountain with Paphnutius, a confessor. Before the monks could tell Antony about her, he told them her story. He would not have her brought in. He said the Lord would heal her where she was.
items.quote: Go, and if she be not dead, you will find her healed
items.witness: The monks went out and found her parents rejoicing and the girl whole.

items.title: Polycratia
items.text: Count Archelaus asked Antony to pray for Polycratia of Laodicea, a Christian young woman in terrible pain in her stomach and side from too much discipline. Antony prayed, and the count wrote down the day. At Laodicea he found her well. He asked when she had recovered.
items.quote: he produced the paper on which he had written the time of the prayer
items.witness: She had been relieved at the time Antony was praying, and all who heard it wondered.

note.text: He did not boast when his prayers were heard, or grumble when they were not. Those who were healed were taught to thank God, not Antony.

more.title: Water in the desert
more.text: He was crossing the desert with monks when the water ran out. The heat was great, and they lay on the ground in despair. Antony went a little way off, knelt and prayed.
more.quote: immediately the Lord made water to well forth where he had stood praying, and so all drank and were revived.

more.title: The crocodiles
more.text: Going to visit the brothers, he had to cross the Arsinoite canal. He prayed, went in with his companions, and all of them crossed safely.
more.quote: the canal was full of crocodiles. And by simply praying, he entered it, and all they with him, and passed over in safety.

more.title: Amun's soul
more.text: Sitting on his mountain, he saw a soul carried up with great joy. He prayed to know whose it was, and a voice told him. Amun lived at Nitria, thirteen days' journey away. The monks marked the day. Thirty days later, brothers from Nitria told them Amun had died that day and hour.
more.quote: This is the soul of Amun, the monk at Nitria.

more.title: The wild beasts
more.text: Wild beasts came for his water and often spoiled his crops. He gently took hold of one of them and spoke to them all. They never came near the place again.
more.quote: Why do you hurt me, when I hurt none of you? Depart, and in the name of the Lord come not nigh this spot.

more.title: A warning to a persecutor
more.text: Balacius, a general who favoured the Arians, beat virgins and flogged monks. Antony wrote to warn him. Balacius laughed, spat on the letter and threw it down. Within five days one of his own horses, the quietest in his stable, pulled him down with a bite and tore his thigh. Three days later he was dead.
more.quote: I see wrath coming upon thee, wherefore cease to persecute the Christians

doubt.title: Doubted, then and now
doubt.text: Athanasius expected doubt. He wrote that many monks agreed in telling such things, and that “we ought not to doubt whether such marvels were wrought by the hand of a man.” In 1877 the scholar Weingarten denied that Athanasius wrote it. The Catholic Encyclopedia says he judged the Life “a mere romance”. The editor of the translation used here, Archibald Robertson, wrote in 1892 that it “swarms with miraculous and demoniacal stories”. He found some of them silly, but he still judged that Athanasius wrote it. By 1907 the Catholic Encyclopedia said the theories against the Life were “abandoned on all hands”.

words.note: His seven letters are not quoted here: we found no free English translation of them. These are his words as others recorded them: Athanasius in the Life, Cassian, and the desert monks in their sayings, which Budge translated from the Syriac in 1907.

feature.q: My book, O philosopher, is the nature of things that are made, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God.
feature.ctx: A philosopher asked him, “How can you endure, father, being deprived of the comfort of books?” Evagrius, a desert monk who died about 400, recorded the answer, and Socrates copied it into his Church History. In Greek, {el|τὸ ἐμὸν βιβλίον, φιλόσοφε, ἡ φύσις τῶν γεγονότων ἐστί}.

quotes.q: If you came to a foolish man, your labour is superfluous; but if you think me prudent become as I am, for we ought to imitate what is good. And if I had come to you I should have imitated you; but if you to me, become as I am, for I am a Christian.
quotes.who: To two Greek philosophers who came to try their skill on him. He spoke through an interpreter.

quotes.q: A man’s life or death cometh from his neighbour; if we benefit our brother we benefit ourselves, and if we offend him we sin against God.
quotes.who: As the desert monks remembered it.

cite.text: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 2, saying 33

quotes.who: His last advice to the two monks who lived with him. He had told the other monks the same.

quotes.q: He who liveth in the desert is free from three kinds of spiritual attacks, that is to say, those which arise through the ears, speech, and sight; he hath only one kind to fight, namely, that of the heart.
quotes.who: As the desert monks remembered it.

cite.text: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 1, chapter 1, saying 46

quotes.q: I saw all the snares of the Enemy laid out upon the ground, and I groaned and said, ‘Who can escape from these?’
quotes.who: In this telling the devils answer him: humility, which they cannot reach.

cite.text: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 1, chapter 10, saying 453

quotes.q: I do not fear God, on the contrary I love Him.
quotes.who: As the desert monks remembered it.

cite.text: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 2, after saying 403

quotes.q: That is not a perfect prayer, wherein a monk understands himself and the words which he prays.
quotes.who: Abba Isaac gives it as his, in Cassian's Conferences.

myths.claim: He foretold our times: a day would come when people go mad, and turn on anyone who is not mad because he is not like them.
myths.truth: It is one of the sayings the desert monks remembered, not something he wrote, and it names no time. Budge's translation of 1907 has “Behold a time shall come to the children of men when they shall become silly”.

cite.text: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 2, saying 179

myths.claim: He is the St Anthony to ask for lost things.
myths.truth: That is a different saint, Anthony of Padua, a Franciscan friar who died in 1231. Britannica says Anthony of Padua “is commonly invoked for the return of lost property”. Merriam-Webster lists the two separately.

cite.text: Britannica, St. Anthony of Padua; Merriam-Webster, Anthony

myths.truth: The Life says he learned from an old man in the next village who “had lived the life of a hermit from his youth up”. The Catholic Encyclopedia thinks he was probably not the first Christian hermit. He is the father of monks because so many followed him.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapter 3; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907

myths.claim: He was a disciple of Paul the Hermit.
myths.truth: Britannica says so, but Athanasius never mentions Paul. In Jerome's story Antony is ninety when he first hears of Paul, and finds him just before Paul dies. The Catholic Encyclopedia says Jerome's account “cannot be used for historical purposes”.

cite.text: Jerome, Life of Paul; Catholic Encyclopedia, 1907

myths.claim: The pig and the bell in his pictures come from his life.
myths.truth: They come from the Hospitallers of St Anthony, an order founded about 1100. Their pigs roamed medieval streets, and they rang bells as they collected alms.

extras.title: Hard questions
extras.lede: Some things in the record are hard to read today. Here they are, plainly.

items.title: Was he black?
items.text: No early source describes the colour of his skin. Athanasius says he was “by descent an Egyptian”, and Sozomen “an Egyptian by race”. He spoke Egyptian, not Greek, and needed an interpreter to talk with Greeks.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapters 1, 16 and 72; Sozomen, Church History, Book 1, chapter 13

items.title: The demon he saw as a black boy
items.text: In the Life, the spirit of lust appears to him “like a black boy, taking a visible shape in accordance with the colour of his mind”. Antony tells it, “thou art black-hearted and weak as a child.” The Life says the black is the colour of the demon’s mind. Scholars see more in it than that. The historians Philip Harland and Maia Kotrosits set this scene beside other Christian stories that picture darker-skinned peoples as demons. In some of them, they write, the result is “a relatively consistent association between darker-skinned natives in isolated regions and demons or the devil.” We give the Life as it has it.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapter 6; Philip A. Harland and Maia Kotrosits, Ethnic Relations and Migration in the Ancient World, 2023

items.title: Hard on the body
items.text: He was ashamed to eat. He never bathed, and would not even put his feet in water unless he had to. He wore a hair shirt until he died. Yet the sayings have him warn against hardship without understanding: “There are some monks who vex their bodies with the labours of abstinence and self-denial, and who, because they have not found understanding, are remote from the path of God.”

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapters 45 and 47; Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 1, chapter 8, saying 296

items.title: No fellowship with heretics
items.text: He would have nothing to do with the Meletians or the Arians. When Arians came to his mountain, “he drove them from the mountain, saying that their words were worse than the poison of serpents.” Dying, he told his monks to keep clear of both. The OCA sums up his charge: “to preserve the Orthodox Faith in its purity”. His editor Robertson warned that even Athanasius would mix some of his own words into “the speeches of his hero”.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapters 68 and 91; OCA; Robertson's introduction

stood.lede: Most lines are Antony's as Athanasius recorded them. Others come from the desert monks' sayings, and one from Evagrius.

quiet.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 2, saying 197

nature.work: Evagrius, as Socrates quotes him in his Church History, Book 4, chapter 23

mystery.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 1, chapter 10, saying 551

circle.name: Athanasius
circle.text: Bishop of Alexandria, and his biographer. When Athanasius was exiled, Antony wrote to Constantine again and again in his defence. In his will he left Athanasius a sheepskin, and the garment he lay on, which Athanasius had once given him new, “which with me has grown old”.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapter 91; Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 31

circle.name: His sister
circle.text: When he gave everything away, he placed his little sister with a community of virgins. Years later he was glad to find her grown old in virginity, and leading other virgins herself.

circle.name: Serapion of Thmuis
circle.text: A bishop. He was with Antony on the mountain when Antony saw visions of what was happening in Egypt. Antony left him the other sheepskin.

circle.name: Amun of Nitria
circle.text: A monk of Nitria who had often stayed at Antony's mountain. Antony saw his soul carried up at the hour he died. In a saying, an Ammon of Nitria asks why Antony's name is better known, when his own labours are greater. Antony answers, “Because I also love the Lord more than thou.”

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapter 60; Sayings of the Desert Fathers, Book 2, saying 180

circle.name: Paul the Simple
circle.text: A peasant of sixty who found his wife with a lover and walked to Antony to become a monk. Antony shut the door on him for three days, then set him to weave mats and unpick them. Paul never grumbled, and Antony made him a monk.

circle.name: Didymus the Blind
circle.text: A learned man who had lost his sight. He came to see Antony when Antony was in Alexandria. Antony asked if he grieved for his eyes, and at last Didymus said he did. Antony said, “I am surprised that a wise man should grieve at the loss of a faculty which he shares with ants and flies and gnats, and not rejoice rather in having one of which only saints and apostles have been thought worthy.”

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: They never met. In Milan, about 386, a visitor named Pontitianus told Augustine about Antony, whose name was new to him. Soon after, weeping under a fig tree, Augustine opened Paul's letters and read the first passage he saw, “for I had heard of Antony”. It was his conversion.

death.big: He died in 356, about 105 years old, on his inner mountain near the Red Sea.
paras: He went to see the monks of the outer mountain one last time. He told them he was near 105 and would not see them again. They wept, and he talked joyfully, “as though sailing from a foreign city to his own”.
They begged him to die among them. He would not. Egyptians then kept the bodies of holy people in their houses, and he had long spoken against it. So he went back to the inner mountain.

A few months later he fell ill. Only his two companions were with him. Palladius names the two who buried him, Macarius and Amatas. He left his sheepskins to Athanasius and Serapion, and his hair shirt to the two.

later.title: Where is his body?
later.text: Athanasius says no one but the two knew the place. Later tradition says it was found under Justinian and taken to Alexandria, then to Constantinople, then to France. The OCA dates the first move to 544 and names Arles in the fifteenth century. His monastery in Egypt calls all this “A False Claim”. It says he still lies in a cave before the southern altar of its old church.

cite.text: The Roman Martyrology (1916), 17 January; OCA; the Monastery of St Antony

items.q: Bury my body, therefore, and hide it underground yourselves, and let my words be observed by you that no one may know the place but you alone. For at the resurrection of the dead I shall receive it incorruptible from the Saviour.
For the rest fare ye well, my children, for Antony is departing, and is with you no more.
items.ctx: Then “he lifted up his feet, and as though he saw friends coming to him and was glad because of them”, he died. His face was joyful.

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox and the Coptic Church count him a saint. The Church of England, the Episcopal Church and the ELCA keep his day too.

churches.note: A memorial on 17 January, as Saint Anthony, Abbot
A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: He longed to die a martyr in 311, but he was not killed. Athanasius says that afterwards he was “daily a martyr to his conscience”. The OCA calls the Life “the first biography of a saint who was not a martyr”.

quotes.q: …St. Anthony, abbot and spiritual guide of many monks. He was most celebrated for his life and miracles, of which St. Athanasius has written a detailed account.
quotes.who: The Roman Martyrology, 1916 edition, for 17 January.

reads.title: The Life of Antony
reads.text: Written within a few years of his death, by a bishop who had seen him many times. Everything else depends on it. The long middle is Antony's own teaching to his monks.

kin.name: Cuthbert of Lindisfarne
kin.text: Bede says he was “affable and pleasant in his character”, and spoke “with cheerful and soothing language, as he was accustomed”. He had long wanted “the secrecy of solitude”, and at last he lived alone on the island of Farne. Made a bishop, he went back after two years to “his much-loved solitude”.

kin.name: Guthlac of Crowland
kin.text: He led a war band for nine years, then became a monk and began “to long for the wilderness”. He spent his last fifteen years as a hermit in the fens, and “evermore sweetness was in his temper”. When two visiting monks hid their ale under a turf, he knew, and asked them “with merry countenance and laughing words” why they had not brought it along.
kin.cite: Felix, Life of St Guthlac, the Old English version

kin.name: Barnabas
kin.text: When the church in Jerusalem was still afraid of Saul, Barnabas, the “Son of Encouragement”, brought him to the apostles. Later he and Paul fell out over Mark, who had once left them. Barnabas wanted to give him a second chance. Paul would not.
